thresholds.viewing_model: GIF shown at 1 image px = 1 CSS px (520 px wide email/chat embed), laptop at ~50 cm: 1 px = 0.2646 mm -> ~0.030 deg visual angle.

hero_cap_height_px.why: The hero headline is the payoff and must read at a glance, not by study. 16 px cap height ~= 0.48 deg cap / ~0.33 deg x-height, i.e. >1.5x the ~0.2 deg critical print size (Legge & Bigelow 2011) and still >= 0.2 deg x-height after a typical mobile down-scale of 520 -> ~340 px (x0.65). It is also ~= WCAG 'large text' (18 pt = 24 px font, cap ~16-17 px), the size WCAG treats as easier to read.

control_label_x_height_px.why: UI label must be read during a ~0.9 s close shot: 9 px x-height ~= 0.27 deg, above the 0.2 deg critical print size (reading speed plateaus above CPS, Legge & Bigelow 2011); comparable to an 18 px UI font, above Apple HIG / Material minimum body sizes (11 pt / 12 sp) at 1x.

cta_x_height_px.why: Secondary result text inside a high-contrast button: 7 px x-height ~= 0.21 deg, just above the 0.2 deg critical print size.

thresholds.ocr: Every key token must be recognised by tesseract 5 (psm 11+6, normal+inverted) on the beat frame. OCR runs on a 3x upscale, so it is a NECESSARY not a sufficient check: take3's full-frame 'boredom' was OCR-readable while its cap height was 10 px; the px threshold is the gate.

sources.title: Legge & Bigelow (2011) Does print size matter for reading? A review of findings from vision science and typography. Journal of Vision 11(5):8
sources.used_for: critical print size ~0.2 deg x-height; fluent range 0.2-2 deg

sources.title: W3C WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) - definition of large text (18 pt / 14 pt bold)
sources.used_for: large-text size reference for the hero threshold

sources.used_for: WCAG sets no absolute px minimum; legibility must be judged at delivered size

thresholds.centering: ROI fully inside crop AND |ROI-centre offset| <= 10% of crop width/height on every close shot.

checks.text: Coffee that tastes like the trail.

mp4_ocr.note: MP4 is 1920 px (3.69x the GIF), so px thresholds are met whenever the GIF meets them

story_test.answer: A coffee brand's landing page in a design tool. The headline reads 'Coffee that tastes like the trail.' with a 'Start a subscription' button. Zoom into a side panel 'Prepared for this design' > Mood with Editorial / SaaS / Playful; the pointer switches SaaS to Playful. The headline then reads 'Bags without the boredom', subhead 'A brighter path from drum to doorstep. Confetti optional.', button 'Let's roast'. For designers/marketers/founders who want to change a page's tone with one control instead of rewriting copy.

story_test.answer: A design tool canvas with several web page mockups; a headline on one mockup changes from 'Coffee that tastes like the trail.' to 'Bags without the boredom'. Something in the right-hand panel is involved but its labels are unreadable.

story_test_method.method: Contact sheet of 16 evenly spaced GIF frames (verify/cold-viewer-contact-sheet.png), no captions, no filenames; question: 'What happened in this clip, and who is it for?'. Pass only if the answer names (1) one Mood control (2) changed the hero copy (3) to a playful voice.
story_test_method.independence: NOT fully independent: graded by the same agent that produced the video (no separate context-free vision model was available in this environment). Treat as provisional; re-run with a fresh vision model given only the contact sheet.
story_test_method.prompt: You are shown 16 frames from an 8-second silent screen recording, in order (left-to-right, top-to-bottom). Describe what happened and who this is for. Do not guess beyond what is visible.
